standard.title: Evaluate source purpose and perspective
standard.description: evaluate primary and secondary sources to determine origin, purpose and perspectives
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4S04 (Analyse data and perspectives): Students analyse data and identify different perspectives in sources. Students can identify viewpoints in sources, but at Year 4 level do not yet evaluate origin and purpose systematically.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students evaluate primary and secondary sources to determine their origin, purpose and the perspectives they present, identifying bias, stereotypes and differences between accounts.

nodes.label: Origin and purpose of sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the origin of a source (who created it, when, where) and explain its likely purpose (to inform, persuade, entertain, record), and explain how origin and purpose might affect the information a source contains.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the origin and purpose of one provided source and explain how these might affect what the source shows.
nodes.typical_width: For a range of primary and secondary sources, identify origin (creator, date, context) and purpose (informative, persuasive, record-keeping), and explain how origin and purpose affect the reliability, completeness and perspective presented in each source.
wider: Compare a primary source (e.g. a colonial-era newspaper article) and a secondary source (e.g. a modern history book) on the same topic, and evaluate how origin and purpose result in different accounts
Investigate how to verify source details — checking publication dates, authorship and institutional affiliation — and evaluate what this reveals about the reliability of different source types
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify origin and purpose cannot evaluate perspective or bias — the evaluative skills in the rest of this descriptor and in AC9HS5S05 depend on understanding that sources are created by someone for a reason that shapes their content.

response_modes.reason: Use a source analysis frame (e.g. Who? When? Why? What does this mean for the information?) to scaffold the move from describing what a source says to analysing what it is and why it was created.

success_criteria: Students identify the origin (creator, date) and purpose of at least one source.
Students explain how the source's origin and purpose might affect what it shows or omits.

nodes.label: Identifying bias and stereotypes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify inferred messages, stereotypes and over-generalisations in historical and contemporary sources, explaining how these reflect the perspective and possible bias of the source's creator.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example of bias or a stereotype in a provided source and explain what perspective it reflects.
nodes.typical_width: Examine visual and written sources (e.g. colonial-era newspaper caricatures, historical photographs, contemporary social media opinions) to identify inferred messages, stereotypes and over-generalisations relating to age, gender, ethnicity, ability, religion or politics; explain what perspective these elements reflect.
wider: Compare a colonial-era source and a contemporary source on the same group (e.g. First Nations Australians, Chinese migrants, women) and explain how the perspectives and stereotypes have changed — or persisted
Analyse how a modern media source about a current issue (e.g. environmental policy, immigration) uses language, image selection and framing to reflect a particular perspective

response_modes.reason: Identifying bias in historical sources — particularly colonial-era sources — requires students to hold a critical distance from the source's viewpoint. Scaffold explicitly: 'What does the creator assume? What is left out? Who might disagree?'

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Colonial-era sources about First Nations Australians, Chinese miners and women provide rich and important territory for bias and stereotype analysis — these are not abstract examples but historically and culturally significant materials that deserve careful analysis.
success_criteria: Students identify at least one example of bias or a stereotype in a source.
Students explain what perspective the bias or stereotype reflects and whose viewpoint it represents.

nodes.label: Comparing accounts and perspectives
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare primary and secondary sources on the same topic to identify similarities and differences in their accounts, explaining why different sources present different perspectives.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two sources on the same topic and identify at least one similarity and one difference in their accounts.
nodes.typical_width: Compare sources of evidence (primary and secondary, from different creators and perspectives) to identify similarities and differences in accounts of the past or present; explain why sources differ and what each perspective reveals; give examples from historical events (e.g. Eureka Stockade, colonial exploration, gold rush).
wider: Compare how an event is described in a source created at the time with how it is described in a recently published account, and evaluate what has changed in the interpretation and why
Examine accounts of the same event from First Nations Australian and European perspectives, and evaluate what each perspective reveals that the other omits

response_modes.reason: Comparing perspectives across multiple source types and historical actors is the core skill — students benefit from practising comparisons across different kinds of differences (time period, cultural background, social position, source type).

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The elaborations name specific rich comparison cases (Eureka Stockade, Burke and Wills, Ned Kelly) where First Nations, colonial and contemporary perspectives differ substantially — these are pedagogically significant and culturally important comparison opportunities.
success_criteria: Students compare at least two sources on the same topic and identify at least one similarity and one difference.
Students explain why the sources might present different accounts.

nodes.label: Evaluating sources for accuracy and perspective
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the accuracy of sources, identify the perspectives they present, and explain how origin, purpose and perspective together affect a source's usefulness for inquiry.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate one source for accuracy and perspective, and explain whether it is useful for a specific inquiry purpose.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate the accuracy and perspectives in a range of primary and secondary sources (checking publication details, author expertise, evidence used, perspectives represented), and explain how origin, purpose and perspective together determine a source's usefulness for inquiry.
wider: Develop and apply a systematic source evaluation criteria framework (e.g. CRAAP test adapted for HASS) to a set of sources on a HASS topic
Evaluate a contested historical event using sources with conflicting accounts, and explain how the conflict between sources can itself be used as evidence of different perspectives

response_modes.reason: Source evaluation at this level requires students to hold multiple analytical frames simultaneously — origin, purpose, perspective, accuracy, and usefulness all interact. Scaffold with structured evaluation protocols before expecting independent application.

success_criteria: Students evaluate at least one source for accuracy and perspective with reference to its origin and purpose.
Students explain whether the source is useful for their inquiry and why.
Students use relevant source analysis terminology (e.g. 'origin', 'purpose', 'perspective', 'bias', 'reliability').
